quote: Müssen die Zahlen der Integritätsbereiche dann immer nothwendig abzählbar sein?
english: Must the numbers of the integral domains then always necessarily be countable?
topic: The page covers systems (number domains) closed under operations, with examples from ring and field theory, questions on when divisibility laws hold in integral domains, and a plan for teaching function theory by combining Weierstrass with Riemann–Cauchy.

triage.modern_statement: Is every integral domain, meaning a commutative ring with 1 and no zero divisors (Hilbert's 'Zahlen der Integritätsbereiche'), necessarily countable as a set? There are two possible readings. (a) For an arbitrary integral domain the answer is no: the real numbers, the complex numbers, and Q(T) with uncountably many indeterminates T are uncountable fields, and therefore uncountable integral domains. (b) If 'Integritätsbereich' means a domain generated over Z by finitely many (or countably many) elements, which is close to how Kronecker used the term, then the answer is yes. Every element is a polynomial expression with integer coefficients in the generators, and there are only countably many such expressions.
triage.answered_by: There is no specific later answer to this note; it follows directly from results Cantor had already published. In 1874 he proved that the real algebraic numbers are countable and that the real numbers are not. Under reading (a), the real numbers (an integral domain) are a counterexample, so the answer is no. Under reading (b), the countability argument is the standard counting of finite polynomial expressions, which is the same kind of argument Cantor used for the algebraic numbers, so the answer is yes. In both readings this is elementary, not a research problem. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem.

evidence.claim: Cantor's 1874 article 'Ueber eine Eigenschaft des Inbegriffes aller reellen algebraischen Zahlen' proves that the set of real algebraic numbers is countable.
In 1874 Cantor showed that the set of real numbers is uncountable, so the real numbers (a field, and therefore an integral domain) are an uncountable integral domain.
Cantor's first uncountability proof appeared in the paper whose main result was the countability of the algebraic numbers.
Finitely generated rings are standard objects; one is generated over Z by finitely many elements, so it is a quotient of a polynomial ring over Z, which is countable.

triage.why: The note asks whether the elements of an integral domain must be countable. Read literally (any integral domain), the answer is no: the real numbers are an integral domain and are uncountable by Cantor's 1874 theorem. If Hilbert meant Kronecker-style domains generated by finitely many quantities, the answer is yes, by the standard counting of polynomial expressions. That second reading is my interpretation from the history of the term; none of the sources I found states it directly. Either way the matter was settled by Cantor's results or by elementary arguments, and it is not a research topic today. Confidence is medium rather than high because the page does not say which meaning of 'Integritätsbereich' Hilbert intended.
